idiom_name: object tag + void (*table[TAG_COUNT][TAG_COUNT])(const void *, const void *)
implementation_notes: C has neither runtime type information nor vtables, so both dispatch axes become explicit data: every object carries a tag (an enum, laid out first in a common initial sequence or union) and dispatch is one lookup in a matrix of function pointers indexed by the two tags. The matrix replaces the classic accept/visit round-trip, and C99 designated initialisers let the cells be written in tag order while unhandled cells stay NULL so they can be reported instead of silently ignored. Use this when the pair itself is the key; the per-type ops-struct variant is better when many operations share one type axis.
pitfalls: A NULL cell is silently a no-op if it is called unguarded: test the pointer and report the pair instead.
Tags and the enum must stay in sync: a module compiled against a stale header builds a valid-looking but wrong table.
Casting arbitrary pointers to a common struct is only defined when the tag lives in the common initial sequence of union members (C11 6.5.2.3); otherwise the dispatch itself is undefined behaviour.

variants.name: Per-type ops struct (hand-rolled vtable)
variants.idiom_name: struct shape_ops of function pointers, one static table per type
variants.implementation_notes: Emulates the object-oriented form: each type owns one static const table of function pointers shared by all of its values, and each value holds a pointer to it, so the first dispatch is an indirect call through ops. The second dispatch is inside the handler, which receives the other object together with its tag because C cannot overload on it. Choose this when one axis is a fixed set of operations over many types; choose the tag-matrix form when the pair itself is the key.
pitfalls: Every constructor must initialise ops; a partially initialised object crashes on the first dispatch.
Casting a handler to a different function-pointer signature is undefined behaviour even when the calling convention happens to line up.
One table per type means adding an operation touches every table: the same cost the object-oriented form pays.
